 1. Description of the component parts
1. Question
It is noted that throughout the nomination dossier, the terms ‘spa town, ‘spa district’, ‘spa’ and ‘historic urban landscape’
are used interchangeably to describe the component parts. In addition, in the supplementary information received on 11
November 2019, it is acknowledged that not all component parts can be said to meet the same definition of ‘spa town’
(Summary file, supplementary information, page 4).
Therefore, ICOMOS would appreciate if the State Parties could provide further information as to what term/concept
could be used to describe all component parts consistently.

1. Response
All component parts may be consistently called “spa towns”, analogous to “historic centres” now enclosed within
modern cities; see Operational Guidelines, Annex 3 page 84-85: Inscription of Historic Towns and Town
Centres on the World Heritage List / (ii) Inhabited historic towns: “To qualify for inscription, towns should
compel recognition because of their architectural interest… To be eligible for inscription in the List, the spatial
organization, structure, materials, forms and, where possible, functions of a group of buildings should essentially
reflect…” […the cultural tradition which has prompted the nomination of the property]. [GSE wording]. The
nomination complies.
The “spa town” is clearly discernible and has been precisely delimited by boundaries in each component part
nominated. Each spa town contains attributes that fall within the timeframe of ca.1700-1930s, the period within
which the greatest developments were made and which reflect the most significant contribution to proposed
OUV. All defined attributes of each spa town collectively reflect urban resorts founded on natural mineral springs
developed for bathing and drinking, integrated with therapeutic, recreational and social facilities. All defined
attributes within the component parts demonstrate the highest levels of authenticity and integrity.
The boundaries of each component part substantially correspond with the boundaries of the “original” spa towns
which today, due to subsequent growth, represent only a part of the current town, although invariably the most
important part. These, in turn, invariably coincide with the activity of the continuing spa tradition. This is
unsurprising since the source of the healing natural mineral water acts as nuclei for the spa function that is
manifest in a specialised urban form. The continuing spa tradition remains alive in the Great Spas and as always
is focussed around the natural source and the historic spa buildings. To not use the term “spa town” for places
known for their historic and continuing spa function would cause confusion, especially with host communities.
This concept was further explained in the November 2019 document “ICOMOS Evaluation 2019. additional
information; summary ref: GA/AS/1613-Add.Inf_1. Response to Question 1, pages 1 to 5.

1

 2. Timeframe
2. Question
ICOMOS understands that the Great Spas of Europe are considered a testimony to the flourishing of the spa phenomenon
in Europe between 1700 and the 1930s. However, it is also noted that some component parts show important periods
of development before and to some extent after that timeframe, which are not included in Figure 11 on page 478 of the
nomination dossier and on page 7 of the summary file of the supplementary information. For instance, Baden bei Wien,
was popular with the Hapsburg Emperors since the fifteen century and hosted important foreign guests like Tsar Peter the
Great in 1698 (page 361). Likewise, Karlovy Vary’s popularity extended across the borders of the Bohemian Kingdom by
the second half of the fifteenth century and a fire in 1604 led to its subsequent reconstruction (page 384). Vichy gained a
widespread curative reputation by the end of the 16th century and its popularity with the aristocracy was high until the
18th century (page 400). In Montecatini Terme, which is considered to testify the last great flourish of the European spa
tradition in the early twentieth century, a number of later interventions are noted namely to the Excelsior Thermal Bath
in 1968, the Redi Thermal Baths in 1964, Viale Verdi in 1963 and the Thermal Institute Grocco in the 1950s (pages
258- 264). Could the States Parties provide further information as to the rationale used to define that timeframe?

2. Response
It may be possible that confusion remains between the concept of a chronologically defined period, ca.17001930s – and the concept of the continuing living tradition. These concepts are not contradictory. Whilst the
continuing spa tradition is an attribute of OUV it is not defined only by the ca.1700-1930s period. The
continuing spa tradition is a value which the Great Spas of Europe accepts; it is an intangible attribute of OUV
that continues beyond the 1930s to the present day and needs to be sustained in the future. However, after the
selected timeframe profound changes were brought upon European cities and society and the pan-European spa
phenomenon changed as a result.
The timeframe of ca.1700-1930s informs and structures the nomination and indicates the principal period in
which the European spa phenomenon flourished and is best represented by the nominated series. It was in this
period that a new urban typology centred on natural mineral springs and designed for the combined medicinal,
social and leisure use of mineral water appeared for the first time in history. This new urban form combines in a
unique way innovative town planning, landscape design, and architecture, and has no earlier parallel. This
period is clearly connected with: the birth of balneology as a scientific discipline (18th C); the first appearance
of dedicated spa-specific structures such as bathhouses, kurhaus, pump rooms and drinking halls, colonnades,
spa pavilions and others (18-19th C); the first planned transformations of a natural landscape into a therapeutic
landscape managed as part of the spa cure (18-19th C); the rise of the middle class leading to the origin of mass
tourism and the erosion of the barriers between class and gender (19th C).
There were of course a number of famous spa locations before 1700, including Karlovy Vary, Spa, Baden bei Wien,
Bad Ems, Baden-Baden and the City of Bath, but it is inaccurate to refer to these in the framework of the
proposed OUV except as context in their history and development. Some of the component parts possess
testimony to their ancient origins and mineral waters which were used in Roman times as well as throughout the
late Middle Ages and Early Modern Times prior to 1700. While tangible heritage of the Roman period is quite
frequent in several component parts, the tangible evidence of the Late Medieval and Early Modern Times is
scarce or buried beneath later historic buildings representative of the timeframe ca.1700 - 1930s. The early
Roman evidence and the few pre-1700 built structures do not contribute directly to the attributes of the
proposed OUV.’

2

 It is acknowledged that the earlier and later significance of the series is important, however it is only after
ca.1700 when spa town development began to attain the appearance and infrastructure of the great spa towns.
Medieval and Renaissance spa locations were not of the spatial plan recognisable in the Great Spas, nor were
many of the specialised building types and public spaces yet developed that would eventually (between ca.1700
and the 1930s) define urbanisation around a medical practice in such an exemplary manner. They were mostly
visited just by a small number of the nobility and were not places reflecting the democratisation of society as in
the later Great Spas. Moreover, balneology as a scientific discipline developed only from the 18th century
following the ideas emanating from the Enlightenment and the first scientific analyses of the natural mineral
waters.
After the 1930s, the pan-European spa phenomenon was different and does not conform to the proposed OUV.
Some of the component parts include modern (post-WWII) interventions that facilitate a living spa tradition
that continues into the twenty-first century.
However, this does not mean that the continuing spa tradition is not important – it is. The continuing spa
tradition has generated some new buildings and structures and modern infrastructure necessary to meet modern
standards of healthcare and hygiene; these new additions are not argued as being part of the proposed OUV.
Continuing spa tradition is important to the character and distinctiveness of all component parts of the Great
Spas of Europe. It is integral to their authenticity, conservation and maintenance, and vital to the local economy
and living communities of the Great Spas of Europe. Continuing spa tradition needs to be sustained by future
management.

3. Justification of criterion (iii)
3. Question
ICOMOS appreciates the information already provided on 11 November 2019 regarding its request in relation to the
justification of criterion (iii) and the living tradition of “taking the cure”. However, it is also noted that little information
is provided in the nominated dossier as to the development of the component parts between the 1930s and the present
moment. ICOMOS also understands from the elements presented in section 3.2 Comparative analysis of the nomination
dossier that the European spa tradition is considered different from other cultural traditions of the use of mineral waters
largely because of its medical use and the innovations it has generated. ICOMOS would be pleased if the States Parties
could provide further clarifications as to how the cultural tradition of ‘taking the cure’, as reflected during the timeframe
of 1700 to the 1930s, compares to how that cultural tradition is reflected nowadays and can still be considered to be living
from a medical perspective. In addition, it would appreciate a clarification on how this medical perspective can be
distinguished from a wellness approach..

3. Response
The Great Spas of Europe bears exceptional testimony to the conscious care for human health that developed
around natural curative mineral waters/springs (thermal and cold). The tradition was born of a remarkable
cultural and social phenomenon that flourished during the selected timeframe. All eleven component Great Spas
have, over many generations of use by patients and visitors, scientifically and medically demonstrated the healing
properties of their waters.

3

 ‘Taking the cure’ refers to the traditional spa function that is designed for healing and health: mainly the use of
healing natural mineral waters (medical definition) for bathing (external treatment), drinking and inhalation
(internal treatment), accompanied by prescribed walks in the therapeutic landscape as well as recreational,
cultural and social activities known as diversions. This combination of medical as well as socio-cultural activities
is a distinctive feature of international spa towns and fashionable baths, of which the Great Spas of Europe are
outstanding examples. ‘Taking the cure’, whether experienced from the ca.1700 to the 1930s or today, is a
personal activity that has always included a mix of medical prescribed procedures and self-care treatments where
therapeutic properties are nonetheless still recognised. We must however further recognise that, historically,
‘taking the cure’ was for the majority fashionable, an activity in some of Europe’s most elegant social and cultural
centres (outside the national capitals) in which to be seen. Many sought a holistic benefit from the wider offer of
the Great Spa, from the waters and the therapeutic landscape, to the opera and casino.
The waters are the same today as they were in the 1700s, and the basic principles of the cultural tradition of
‘taking the cure’ also remain much the same. The Great Spas reflect continuing trends in medical care and
continue to actively participate in medical research. They continue to innovate; the tradition can therefore be
clearly seen to be living from a medical perspective. The Great Spas continue to provide multiple external and
internal medical treatments for a wide range of ailments (including many ‘new’ medical conditions not known
or identified during the ca.1700-1930s timeframe) through bathing, drinking, inhalation and other specialised
peloid treatments, such as moor and peat baths and mud (fango).
In this, health visits to the Great Spas may last from two to even four weeks. Non-medicalised use of the mineral
waters (thermal and cold) continue to be offered for non-prescriptive shorter stays (from one day to a few days),
involving self-treatment, revitalisation, wellness or a preventive approach. The medical approach, and the wellness
approach, have been taking place side by side in the Great Spas for centuries. However, while the medical
perspective (of spa towns) is built on the use of natural curative mineral waters/springs, wellness activities can
take place anywhere and often utilise water from the mains supply (tap water) which is anathema to the
European spa tradition. While the Great Spas are the exemplar of urbanisation around a medical practice, their
function and facilities stretch beyond medical exclusivity. It is still the natural and sustainable spa water and the
features of the Great Spas, however, that will always bring guests to ‘take the cure’.
The Great Spas also continue to maintain a vibrant offer in healthy sporting activities (golf, tennis, swimming,
equestrian, etc) and entertainment (casinos, theatre, opera, music, etc.), and continue to provide multi-faith and
multi-denominational religious facilities, especially for foreign guests. Moreover, such activity substantially takes
place in historic facilities that are sustained in their original function. The Great Spas are designed urban walking
centres that integrate a seamless transition into well-maintained formal and informal green spaces and finally the
wider recreational and therapeutic landscape, known as the ‘terrain cure’. All are free to use these public spaces,
for medical, recreational and wellness purposes, by long-standing tradition.
The concept of continuing tradition is a value that informs the OUV, directs the management of the property,
and remains pivotal to economic sustainability. This continuing tradition however does not detract or divert
emphasis from the heyday of the Great Spas between ca.1700 and the 1930s as reflected in the nomination
dossier.
[In Section 3 of the Annex attached to this Summary there is further information supplied by individual
component spa towns giving a wide range of examples as to how the continuing living tradition of the Great Spas
of Europe manifests itself today and has continued to evolve beyond the heyday of ca.1700-1930s There is also
additional commentary and examples of further developments in spa medicine and how this remains distinct and
contrasts with the current wellness approach prevalent across the global spa industry.]

4

 4. Comparative analysis
4. Question
4a. ICOMOS appreciates the supplementary information provided on 11 November 2019 regarding the criteria used

for creating a hierarchy for the selection of component parts presented in pages 148 to 150 (Annex file, supplementary
information). However, ICOMOS considers that some of the criteria presented in the table on page 148 are quite broad
and difficult to assess. It is also understood that the number of spa guests, the numbers of hotels, numbers of churches of
different denomination and choice of diversion were analysed. Therefore, could the States Parties provide details on how
the ranking provided in page 150 was done and to what extent this ranking derives from the application of the scoring
assigned to the criteria on page 148?

4b. In addition, could the States Parties further explain how the established criteria will be taken into account to be
consistent for possible future additions to the series?

4. Response
4a. It has to be stressed that the analysis of the Spa Lexicon by Flechsig (1883) was only prepared as part of the

additional information provided to ICOMOS on 11 November 2019 in order to further support the selection of
the 11 component parts of the Great Spa Spas of Europe made by means of the comparative analysis. However, it
has to be understood that the Spa Lexicon was published in 1883 and, therefore, does not reflect the important
latter part of the heyday of the European spa phenomenon. This occurred at the turn of the 19th and 20th
centuries, prior to World War I, and finally during the 1920/30s, which was associated with significant new
development not only in prominent spa towns of the 1880s but also with re-birth of older spa towns such as
Montecatini Terme. Therefore, the ranking presented on page 150 of the additional information does not have any
direct link to the selection criteria adopted when preparing the Nomination Documentation.
This selection was a result of a long demanding process which started as early as 2008 when the first
comparative analysis of 89 important spa towns in 17 European countries was published by Czech spa expert
Lubomír Zeman followed by a comparative study prepared by German spa expert Andreas Förderer for an
international conference in Baden-Baden held by the German national committee of ICOMOS in 2010. The
latter included a shortlist of 17-22 spa towns to be included in a potential transnational serial nomination of
European spa towns and included all 11 towns that are now component parts of the Great Spas of Europe. In
2014, a group of 16 spa towns was placed on the Tentative Lists of 7 European countries.
Decisive for the final selection of the GSE group was the work undertaken between 2014 and 2016 by an
independent group of spa experts representing the Czech Republic, France, Germany and the UK who were
commissioned to prepare a global thematic study and a European comparative analysis. The analysis was made
on a sample of 45 most important European spa towns and ended with a recommendation to further reduce the
number of spa towns for a serial transnational nomination.
The framework used by the expert group to assess the component parts of the nominated property followed five
key criteria (divided into eight questions) that were used as the basis for the analysis of European spa towns (as
shown on page 148 of the additional information). The experts had to assess whether the evaluated spa towns:

5

 Description and history.
1) make a significant contribution to the historical development of the specific type of settlement that is
the European spa town in the long 19th century;
Water/springs and use.
2) possess outstanding evidence for the historical development of European spa bathing and drinking
culture due to their healing springs and their use;
Urban structure.
3) possess a historical metropolitan urban structure that reflects the form and function of a great
European spa town with different quarters (spa quarter, residential areas with villas, closed urbanistic
extensions) intensively mixed with different parks and green spaces and with connection to the
surrounding landscape used for recreation and as part of the cure;
4) feature a wide and diverse range of high-quality historical buildings characteristic of the spa
(“Kurhaus”, pump rooms, covered walks, bathing establishments), historical hotel buildings and other
elements of a modern metropolitan touristic infrastructure;
International standing.
5) verifiably enjoyed a reputation as a “global spa”, the chosen destination of a significant international
clientele (both in number and composition) which functioned as a role-model for other spa towns in
the long 19th century;
6) were repeatedly a major scene of significant political events in the European history of the long 19th
century and were the place of origin, or provided the topic, of works of art (literature, music, painting)
of outstanding universal significance;
Authenticity and integrity.
7) possess a high level of authenticity and integrity of the historic town structure and morphology (in its
ground plan and elevation and as to the wholeness of the ensemble) as well by its stock of historical
buildings;
8) feature a high level of authenticity and integrity of the continuing function as an international spa
town.
For each question, one point (low ranking), three points (normal ranking) or five points (high ranking) could be
assigned to each spa town which meant that 40 points was the maximum which could be obtained by each spa
town. The evaluations of individual experts were then averaged, thus creating the overall ranking of the evaluated
spa towns which became the basis for selection of the GSE group. Finally, a further integrity test was applied
during which spa towns were excluded which had lost their continuing spa function or where their structural
integrity was compromised (e.g. Wiesbaden, Aix-les-Bains, Plombières-les Bains, Buxton or Bad Homburg).

6

 As a result, the States Parties agreed a final selection of 11 spa towns to go forward in the serial transnational
nomination to be submitted to UNESCO.

4b. The selection of component parts involved a strict and robust procedure, the outcome of which involved

some de-selection and, therefore, does not currently anticipate any likely additions in the future. If in the
unlikely circumstances of a further State Party bringing forward a proposed additional component to this series
then exactly the same criteria and procedure would apply to its assessment as was previously applied during the
comparative analysis study and the selection process. This unlikely situation has been anticipated when preparing
the Management System and the Project Management Plan. The following extract is from the ND vol.3 PMP
pg. 14, final paragraph says:
… “At the request of a State Party to the World Heritage Convention, the IGC (Intergovernmental Committee)
will ask the GSMB (Great Spas Management Board) to examine the possibility of adding to the serial inscription.
The GSMB will subsequently make a recommendation to the IGC on any proposal to extend the transnational
serial inscription. The IGC, who require a unanimous decision concerning a proposed extension, will then
instruct the GSMB to assist with any new inscription procedure if a State Party bringing forward such a
proposed extension to the GSE inscription so wishes, having in all cases taken advice from the World Heritage
Centre.”

5. Boundaries
5. Question
5a. ICOMOS notes that the boundaries of the City of Bath do not seem to follow the same rationale, based on the

mapping of key attributes, used for the other component parts. Could the States Parties provide further information as to
the rationale used for defining the boundaries of this component?

5b. ICOMOS also notes that parts of the boundaries of some component parts, namely Vichy and Montecatini Terme are
drawn through the axis of streets and considers that this should be changed to include both sides of the streets.

5c. In addition, in some component parts, the boundaries of the nominated component parts only slightly differ from

existing protective designations (at the national, regional or provincial level). For instance, this is the case of Baden bei
Wien, where the northern part of boundaries of the protection zone according to the Construction Plan only presents
minor differences from those of the nominated property (page 8 of Atlas IV). In Bad Ems, the boundary seems to include
part of the conservation area north of the listed garden but not the northwest part of the conservation area (page 66 of
Atlas IV). Similarly, for Baden-Baden, the north boundary and part of the central area of the conservation area seems
to only slightly defer from that of the nominated property (page 78 Atlas IV). In Montecatini Terme, and as mentioned
before, the western boundary of the nominated property is drawn through the middle of the street however it is noted that
part of built fabric to the west has a preservation statute (page 104 of Atlas IV). In such cases, ICOMOS would
appreciate further information whether the boundaries of the nominated component parts could be revised to coincide with
existing designations in order to facilitate management.

5d. Regarding Vichy, and based on information provided by the technical evaluation mission, ICOMOS would like to

enquiry why the railway station was not included in the boundary of the nominated property since it seems to have served
as a pivot to the extension of the town.

7

 5e. Could the States Parties also explain if the northern boundary of Karlovy Vary could be extended to ensure an
adequate level of protection from future development, particularly from a visual perspective?

5. Response
5a. The State Party of the UK and the City of Bath have, after careful consideration issued a Boundary

Statement which is contained in full in the Annex, section 5.a. In this Statement it is argued that there is a
compelling need to keep the proposed boundary of the component part, Bath as a spa (Great Spas of Europe), to
match the boundary of the existing World Heritage Site, the City of Bath. The rational for this is to ensure the
effective management of the property as required by the Operational Guidelines.

5b.1 Vichy; accepts ICOMOS’s request and has modified its boundaries to include the plots (in their entirety)

located on either side of the street (see new maps, Annex, section 5.b.). This change is reflected in particular by
the integration of heritage elements originally excluded including the railway station and the synagogue. The
proposed revisions to the component property and buffer zone maps of Vichy are contained in the Annex, section
5.b. These changes have been agreed between the State Party and the municipal authorities of Vichy.

5b.2 Montecatini Terme;the State Party wishes to confirm that the property boundaries that ran down the

middle of certain streets have been moved in order to include both sides of the streets. New maps have been
prepared accordingly and are contained in the annex of supplementary information in Section 5.b.2a maps 1 – 11

5c.1 Baden bei Wien; has prepared a Statement with the State Party which combines its response to question 5c.
along with that to 6b. which relates to buffer zones in particular. This Statement contains further justification of
the current component property and buffer zone boundaries and their relationship to existing protection
provision which is listed. (see Annex, section 5.c.1).

5c.2 Bad Ems; has prepared a Statement in conjunction with the Federal State of Rhineland-Palatinate

concerning the proposed boundaries of the component property and describes how the new continuous cultural
monument zone “Historic Spa Bad Ems” provides protection including the entire nominated component part.
(see Annex, section 5.c.2)

5c.3 Baden-Baden; has prepared a Statement in conjunction with the Federal State of Baden-Württemberg

confirming that the status quo of the boundary of the nominated property and conservation area is appropriate
and adequate for facilitating management. The revised boundary of the Conservation Area of Baden-Baden
encompassing the nominated property in its entirety came into effect on 1st November 2018. The boundary
shown in the map provided on page 78, Atlas IV, was valid until 31st October 2018, and has already been
superseded by the map on page 177, Baden-Baden Local Management Plan. The justification for the slight
difference between the nominated property, and the north boundary and part of the central boundary of the
revised conservation area is provided in the Statement. (see Annex, section 5.c.3 and the file of maps from BadenBaden).

5c.4 Montecatini Terme; The west part of built fabrics out of the nominated property is subjected to the

protection measures indicated as “preservation statute” (page 104 atlas IV), corresponding to the historic
centre area (zone A) identified by the current municipal Urban Planning Regulation, like the area included in the
boundary of component of Montecatini. However, In the western area out of the boundary there are much less
density of buildings dating back to the reference timeframe, and the original features are less present, due to the
fact that buildings have undergone major transformations over time. While, in the nominated area there is the

8

 highest density of buildings dating back to the reference timeframe, buildings that largely retain the typological,
formal and original material characteristics. Furthermore, many of the buildings present in this area are more
directly connected, also because of their function, to the theme of the spa town

5d. Vichy; agrees to include the station within the perimeter of the property and considers that the best way to

attach it to the property is to include the rue de Paris, which has always been the main axis leading spa guests to
the spa district (see new maps, Annex, section 5.b.).

5e. Karlovy Vary; the municipal authority has prepared a Statement concerning the possibility of extending the
northern boundary of the buffer zone if necessary. A justification of the current proposal is also explained. (see
Annex, section 5.e).
[There is additional information concerning this section in the Annex]

6. Protection and Management system
6. Question
6a. ICOMOS understands that the Czech component parts are protected in their entity as Urban Heritage Reserves by

the Act no. 20/1987 Coll (page 665 of the nomination dossier) and that the component part of Vichy is almost entirety
protected as part of the ‘Site Patrimonial Remarquable’. However, the other component parts do not seem to be protected
in their entirety in similar ways. For instance, in Spa the ZPU only covers parts of the nominated property (page 17
of Atlas IV); in Bad Ems, Baden-Baden and Bad Kissingen, the conservation areas only cover parts of the nominated
property; and in Montecatini Terme, the preservation statute only covers part of the component part (page 104 of Atlas
IV). Whilst ICOMOS understand that other protective measures might apply, it would nevertheless appreciate further
information on whether the legal protection, from a heritage perspective, could be extended to the entirety of all or most of
the component parts, in line with what is in place for the Czech components?

6b. ICOMOS also notes that the buffer zones of the component parts seem to be mainly protected by a mosaic of

environmental and natural designations and instruments and would appreciate a concise explanation on how the buffer
zone of each component part is protected, from a legal and cultural heritage perspective, and if such measures cover the
buffer zone in its entirety.

6c. A number of elements of the management system seem not to be fully in place yet or are still being developed.

ICOMOS would appreciate further information on when such elements (e.g., the local management plans, and the
appointment of the site managers/coordinators) will be finalised and start being implemented.

6d. Could the States Parties also clarify, in a concise way, the legal status of the local management plan for each
component part and its articulation with other existing planning documents?

6. Response
6a. All seven States Parties participating in this serial transnational nomination manage existing World

Heritage Sites and have sophisticated and multi-layered legislation in place to ensure the highest level of
protection is given to OUV. The extent of this legislation was submitted with the nomination (ND vol.2 Chapter
5 pg. 644ff and accompanying digital discs) and was also outlined in the Management System which included
the Property Management Plan and 11 Local Management Plans, one for each component part. Each State

9

 Party has evolved its own legislation for the protection of World Heritage and no two States Parties carry this
out in exactly the same way. However, each remain confident in their ability to provide adequate and
comprehensive protection to World Heritage as necessary.
The Annex (see section 6a) contains Statements from a number of States Parties and Federal States. The Czech
Republic provides comprehensive protection for the entirety of a World Heritage Site and all other States Parties
and Federal States use their raft of protective measures embodied in national and federal heritage legislation to
ensure equal and matching levels of protection across the whole series.

6b. Each component part (spa town) has responded to the request from ICOMOS to clarify the legal and

cultural heritage protection and controls that apply to the proposed buffer zones. All have responded with clear
information and this has been collated in section 6.b of the attached Annex document and the file of maps from
Baden-Baden.

6c. and 6d. The answer to these two questions had been combined in one section 6c & 6d in the Annex. All

component parts have responded and described the current status and legal standing of the Local Management
Plans within the frameworks of heritage and landscape protection and urban planning prevalent within each
State Party. Each component has also clarified the current status of the acting Site Managers, some of whom are
already permanent posts, others being temporary or part-time. As the function of the LMPs and the role of the
Site Managers is dedicated to the management of World Heritage the adoption of the plans and the
confirmation of a permanent staffing structure are both contingent on the Great Spas of Europe being inscribed on
the World Heritage list. [There is additional information concerning this section in the Annex]

7. Monitoring
7. Question
7a. ICOMOS understands that mineral springs are regularly monitored but that, at present, monitoring of the built

fabric is mainly limited to listed buildings. It also understands that a common format for assessing the state of
conservation of the component parts has been developed based on six types of attributes. However, some of the ‘measures’
associated with the defined indicators seem quite difficult to assess such as ‘character of spa historic urban landscape to
remain unchanged’ or, in relation to the therapeutic and recreational landscape, ‘links to remain unchanged’. The proposed
periodicity for some of the monitoring measures (e.g., twice within each Periodic Reporting cycle) also looks insufficient.
ICOMOS would appreciate if the States Parties could provide further details on how the proposed indicators could be
reinforced in relation to the weaknesses noted.

7b. ICOMOS also notes that monitoring indicators related to tourism are limited to ‘number and type of accommodation

units’. It also understands that not all components have visitor management plans per se or sustainable tourism strategies
and that a more coherent approach to visitor management across the whole property will be developed if the nomination is
successful. Therefore, ICOMOS is interested in knowing if a timetable for developing those instruments already exists or
when it is envisaged to start being developed.

10

 7. Response
7a. Monitoring of built fabric and the component parts as a whole is crucial for future management and is

the reason for the indicators suggested in the ND. The need to develop further the monitoring methodology is
recognized in the Property Management Plan and its associated Action Plan, (see i) Chapter 5e, pg. 775ff of the
ND, ii) PMP, vol 3 of ND, pg. 41, 4.10.1 Joint Monitoring – to improve methodology and to share best practice,
and iii) PMP Action Plan pg. 51 actions MP6 & MP7 concerning training, harmonization and timetable to
bring about improved and unified monitoring procedures.)
In the case of all component parts, tried and tested mechanisms and instruments for monitoring the state of
conservation of the urban fabric and natural environment of the nominated property and buffer zone exist. This
provides for an effective multi-tiered and multi-disciplinary urban governance system that forms a solid basis for
sustainable management of a future UNESCO World Heritage site. The appraisal of ‘character’ is a common
feature of urban and landscape conservation studies and protection and has influenced design and planning
guidelines for decades. These principles will be employed in the assessment of the state of conservation of the
groups of attributes as identified in the nomination dossier and which justify OUV. These groupings are clearly
logical when assessing the character of the specific components that are the Great Spas of Europe.
It is proposed to expand on the description of these groupings further in order to more precisely define the
measures in the table on p. 954 of the ND. All towns have a detailed listing of all types of accommodation
available and an estimation of room occupancy.
For example relating to Attribute 2. “Spa historic urban landscape” to replace the term ‘Character of spa
historic urban landscape to remain unchanged’ with the more defined measure of; ‘Preserving all physical elements as
described in Section 2a and in the table on page 954 of the ND, in order to ensure that the overall characteristics of the
historic urban landscape of the spa town remain unaltered and are maintained in good condition to ensure that OUV is
protected.’
For a further example relating to Attribute 4. “ Therapeutic and recreational spa landscape” to replace the
monitoring measure of the percentage of green open space, the linkages and characteristics to remain unchanged,
with - ‘Preserving the visual and/or functional links within the physical elements as described in Section 2a and in the
table on page 954 of the ND in order to ensure that the landscape areas remain unchanged, other than the restoration and
maintenance of planting schemes, especially those that belong to designed landscapes and public open space that contribute
to the qualities and setting of the urban structure and important features within the setting.’
In the Czech Republic the State Party monitors the activities continuously through the national monitoring
mechanism which is based on reports prepared by the National Heritage Institute for the Ministry of Culture.
In Germany the National Committee of ICOMOS monitors World Heritage Sites continuously and writes
annual reports concerning the condition of the properties. For the Great Spas a biennial period of monitoring
has now been recommended as more desirable than once every three years and this has been accepted by the
States Parties.

7b. Tourism is a well-defined and understood activity within all component spa towns which has a long-term
relationship with the visitor economy and management. Tourism is a significant element of economic
development policy in all component parts and each has a structure to manage, monitor and promote tourism
activity within the municipal structures, usually on a local basis in the large and medium sized towns but
sometimes managed on a regional basis in the smaller towns. All component parts gather annual tourism data

11

 although this is not on a consistent and comparative basis across all spa towns at this stage. All spa towns have a
sustainable tourism strategy in place or in development. (see Annex, section 7.b.) The harmonisation of all
available tourism data in the future is a priority of the Action Plan within the overall Property Management
Plan.
Data includes total number of visitors with a split between staying visitors and day trips, in the larger towns this
is further analysed to provide the number of overnights and the average length of stay, combined with a record
of the country of origin of ‘foreign’ (European and non-European) visitors. A minority of spa towns also have
detailed information concerning health visitors; those on national health provision or private patients and this
is combined with the length of stay and the type of accommodation used. All towns have a detailed listing of all
types of accommodation available and an estimation of room occupancy.
The tourism officers representing each spa town meet as a sub-group and are currently developing a Marketing
strategy for the Great Spas of Europe (a draft is available if required). Joint promotion already takes place with a
presence planned for the ITB Exhibition in Berlin in March 2020, the largest travel and tourism trade show in
Europe.
The larger spa towns within the Great Spas have existing and sophisticated Destination Management
Organisations (DMOs), having been established over decades, with a professional coherent approach to visitor
management across the whole property. Sustainable tourism strategies and marketing plans already exist and as a
result all spa towns are aware of today´s challenges posed by excessive tourism and the high impact of day visits.
The members of the Great Spas are ready to promote the common property and brand within a framework of
sustainable tourism that will protect and enhance, not damage, the essence of these important spa towns.
